title: Intrapartum Synthetic Oxytocin as a Potential Mediator for Postpartum Depression
content: Background: Despite negative impacts on mothers, the pathophysiology of postpartum depression (PPD) is poorly understood. Due to social behavior modulation contribution, synthetic oxytocin (synOT) has been routinely used to augment or induce labor. Aim: The present study examined the association between intrapartum synOT administration and maternal PPD using a prospective design from the second day postpartum. We hypothesized that women exposed to intrapartum synOT would have a reduced risk of PPD compared with those without synOT administration. Methods: The study was conducted in Obstetrics & Gynecology Department, from our University Emergency County Hospital, between August 2019 and April 2021. We included 904 women and according to Edinburg Postpartum Depression Scale, 26.10% have PPD and 73.89% did not have PPD. Considering augmentation or labour induction, about 609 (67.36%) women received synOT during the intrapartum period and 295 (32.63%) women didn’t receive synOT intrapartum. Demographic characteristics of the participants (i.e., age, parity, ethnicity, delivery type, and postpartum hospitalization days) were assessed. Results: Our results show that the rate of PPD was lower in women with synOT administration in comparison with women without synOT administration (20.9% vs. 37.10%, p<0.001). It was shown also that women with synOT administration were much younger, and the major were primiparous in comparison with those without synOT administration (p<0.001). There was also a statistical significance in ethnicity from both women with or without synOT administration in the favor of Romanian women (p=0.01). Interestingly, the major of the women with synOT administration had spontaneously delivery in comparison with those without synOT administration (74.38% vs. 6.77%, p<0.001) and less postpartum hospitalization days (0.43% vs. 0.93%, p<0.001). Conclusions: Our study sustained that synOT could represent a potential mediator on the PPD prevalence. These results suggest that intrapartum synOT administration may offer a potential benefit to mothers at risk of PPD.
